export-urn-li-share-6452512243320967169.caption:
This week, world leaders are gathered in New York to discuss the growing epidemic of tuberculosis (TB) and the increasing burden non-communicable diseases (NCDs), the first time in history that there are two High-Level Meetings on health during a UN General Assembly. These meetings are a pivotal opportunity to step up the pace to match the ambition of the 2030 Agenda
Progress and investments on both TB and NCDs to date remains insufficient.  TB infects more than 10 million new people every year and claims 4500 lives every day. NCDs account for 70 percent of the world’s deaths, killing 15 million people between the ages of 30 and 69 every year. At the same time, half the world lacks access to essential health services. 
UNDP is working with partners to drive multi-sectoral action and partnerships across government, the UN system, private sector, civil society and academia. For example, UNDP partners with the Global Fund to support and strengthen multi-sectoral responses to TB in 22 countries by providing integrated policy, programme and capacity development support. To date, this has resulted in 888,398 TB cases being successfully treated.  Increasing access to TB diagnosis and treatment, and ensuring no-one is ‘left behind’, is a priority. To raise awareness of these issues in the lead up to the high level meeting, we are communicating on our work in Tuvalu where UNDP, the Global Fund and the Red Cross are working closely with the Government to address the barriers to healthcare remote communities face , by bringing TB diagnosis and treatment directly into peoples communities and homes. #UNDP

export-urn-li-share-6452602839968608256.caption:
These numbers present us with a huge challenge. However, at UNDP we have made a commitment to work for a Latin America and the Caribbean, with peaceful, non-violent societies and where any type of discrimination against women and girls - of which violence is the harshest expression - is not tolerated. That is why we are very happy for this morning’s launch of the Spotlight Initiative for #LatinAmerica on the margin of the General Debate of the 73rd UN General Assembly with UN and government top officials. The joint EU/UN $500 million-euro initiative will work to accelerate efforts to end violence against women and girls (EVAWG) around the world. The Spotlight Latin America programme, which will fund targeted interventions in five (5) Spotlight countries (Argentina, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Mexico) to improve the rights of women and girls, helping them to live lives free from violence with a view to eradicating #femicide in Latin America. The Latin America programme will also include a regional component aimed at sharing the successful practices and lessons learnt, while replicating relevant programmes throughout the region.

In Latin America, UNDP has partnered with UN Women, UNFPA, UNICEF and other partner agencies, in a work that will focus on the elimination of the violence against women and girls, and in particular the fight against femicide, through strengthening and implementation of laws and public policies, work with state institutions to improve their response; prevention through evidence-based programs and campaigns, the establishment of essential services for victims and survivors; the collection and use of data on the prevalence and incidence of cases of violence against women and girls and quality, disaggregated and comparable femicides; and the work and strengthening of civil society organizations in their work in the elimination of violence against women and girls and femicide.

Specifically, UNDP will use its expertise and comparative advantage to support the adaptation and strengthening of normative frameworks and public policies for the elimination of VAWG and femicide, the strengthening of institutions in the generation and analysis of data that relate citizen security with violence against women and girls, including the adoption of an indicator of femicide. In addition, UNDP will make available to the countries of the region good practices and evidence to inform the design of public policies, for example, in situations of generalized violence; and strengthening the capacities of security and justice systems to provide services to victims.

Violence against women and girls is one of the most widespread and devastating human rights violations globally. It exists in all countries and communities across generations and socio-economic strata, and is a major obstacle to achieving gender equality and sustainable development, as articulated in the #2030Agenda for Sustainable Development: https://goo.gl/z8YtyU #UNDP
